She has no other major comorbidities and asks about research in which rapamycin improved vaccine responses in older adults. Which pathway effect does Hazzard identify in this research?

highlightAliases.new: Influenza. With less antibody production after standard vaccination, increasing the antigen dose or adding an adjuvant can improve the response. In the trial described, high-dose vaccine gave 24% relative efficacy against laboratory-confirmed influenza with protocol-defined influenza-like illness compared with standard dose. Antibody titers and clinical illness are different outcomes (p59–60; DíazGranados et al., NEJM 2014, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1315727).

highlightAliases.old: Influenza high-dose/adjuvanted formulations can improve responses. One trial found 24% relative efficacy for high-dose versus standard-dose vaccine against influenza-like illness (p60).
highlightAliases.new: Influenza high-dose/adjuvanted formulations can improve responses. One trial found 24% relative efficacy for high-dose versus standard-dose vaccine against laboratory-confirmed influenza with protocol-defined influenza-like illness (p60; DíazGranados et al., NEJM 2014).

highlightAliases.old: Low-dose rapamycin/mTOR inhibition, senolytics and metformin are discussed as research approaches; the chapter does not establish routine anti-aging prescriptions (p60, p62).
highlightAliases.new: The influenza vaccine study used everolimus (RAD001), a rapamycin derivative that inhibits mTOR. It measured antibody responses in older adults. The separate rapamycin longevity experiments were in mice. These findings support research into mTOR biology; they do not provide a clinical indication to prescribe an anti-aging treatment (pp. 60, 62). Original human trial.

highlightAliases.old: Helper T-cell lineages support intracellular pathogen defense, antibody production in follicles and other specialized responses. Regulatory T cells restrain activation. Tissue-resident memory T cells can provide a rapid local response. Aging affects these populations differently, and peripheral blood findings need not describe their behavior in tissue (p57–58).

highlightAliases.old: The mechanisms underlying inflammaging remain incompletely understood, but are hypothesized to include activation of innate immune PRRs by PAMPs arising from chronic infections (such as viral infections with herpesvirus family members, or HIV infection, which is associated with increased inflammatory parameters even in individuals with nondetectable viral loads); in addition, age-associated accumulation of DAMPs such as noncellassociated nucleic acids, mitochondria, ATP, urate crystals, heat shock proteins, ceramide, hyaluronan, amyloid, and others resulting from cellular or tissue damage leads to activation of innate immune PRRs such as TLRs and the NLRP3 inflammasome.

highlightAliases.old: In vivo tissue context is likely to be an important factor; for example, evaluation of TLR function in monocytederived DCs showed an age-associated increase in cytokine production; such DCs are derived from monocytes using growth factors and cytokines (GM-CSF and IL-4), and could model DCs generated in the context of inflammation.

highlightAliases.old: Thus, ageassociated impairment in cytokine production could reflect inflammatory dysregulation and an inability to further increase cytokine levels beyond a basal level in response to a newly encountered antigen (such as a PAMP from a pathogen or vaccine).
